question: What is the best way for a nurse to find out how much pain a patient is feeling?

options.A: Asking the patient and listening to them
options.B: Looking at the size of the injury
options.C: Watching for changes in resting pulse

explanation: Pain is personal! Only the patient truly knows what they are feeling, so their word is always our best guide.

question: Why might a patient have normal vital signs even when they are in severe pain?

options.A: Chronic pain only triggers the calming nervous system
options.B: Vital signs only change if internal organs are damaged
options.C: The body's stress system gets used to the ongoing discomfort over time
options.D: Brainstem receptors block all body changes

explanation: When pain lasts, the body adapts. Blood pressure and pulse can settle back to normal, so never assume a patient is pain-free just because their vitals look fine!

question: What is the medical term for when nerve endings turn tissue damage into an electrical signal?
explanation: Think of transduction as the translation step—turning a painful physical injury into an electrical message that travels up the nerves.

question: How do A-delta nerve fibers behave differently from C nerve fibers?

options.A: A-delta fibers only react to emotional stress
options.B: A-delta fibers only work inside the brain and spinal cord
options.C: A-delta fibers carry dull aches over a long time
options.D: A-delta fibers are wrapped in myelin and carry sharp pain very quickly

explanation: Because A-delta fibers have a protective coating (myelin), they rush the message to your brain, giving you that immediate sharp sting right when you get hurt.

question: What main feature sets chronic pain apart from acute pain?

options.A: It happens without any tissue damage
options.B: It lasts longer than three to six months
options.C: It starts only in the outer nerves
options.D: It never responds to any medication

explanation: Acute pain heals up quickly, but chronic pain sticks around long past the normal healing time, usually defined as lasting over 3 to 6 months.

question: A patient feels a burning, shooting pain down their leg after a back injury. What kind of pain is this?
explanation: Burning, tingling, or shooting pains are classic signs of neuropathic pain, which happens when nerves themselves are irritated or damaged.

question: Which pain scale is best to use for a baby or toddler who cannot speak yet?
explanation: Since babies can't tell us their pain score, we use the FLACC scale to watch their body language, facial expressions, and crying instead.

question: In the OLD CARTS pain assessment guide, what does the letter 'C' stand for?

options.B: Character or quality of the pain

explanation: The 'C' asks 'What does it feel like?'—is it stabbing, aching, burning, or throbbing?

question: How do non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) mainly work in the body?

options.A: By putting the central nervous system to sleep
options.B: By releasing natural endorphins in the spine
options.C: By attaching straight to brain opioid receptors
options.D: By blocking prostaglandins at the injury site

explanation: NSAIDs like ibuprofen stop the body from making prostaglandins—the chemical helpers that cause swelling and pain right where you got hurt.

question: What is the main difference between physical dependence on a drug and psychological addiction?

options.A: Addiction stops the moment you lower the dose
options.B: Dependence only happens to people who abuse drugs
options.C: Dependence is a normal body adaptation, while addiction involves strong cravings
options.D: Dependence stops future pain relief from working

explanation: Physical dependence just means your body gets used to a medicine and reacts if you stop too fast. Addiction is a brain disease marked by compulsive cravings and loss of control.

question: Which of these is a physical, non-drug method to help ease pain?

options.B: Applying a cold pack to a fresh sprain
options.D: Giving a dose of oral paracetamol

explanation: Using physical items like heat packs, cold packs, or gentle massage are great non-drug ways to soothe sore tissues.

question: How do relaxation and distraction techniques help reduce a patient's pain?

options.A: They destroy nociceptor nerves in the skin
options.B: They permanently change pain chemicals in the blood
options.C: They stop the liver from breaking down pain meds
options.D: They trigger nerve pathways that block pain signals at the spinal cord

explanation: Think of the 'gate control theory'—calming or distracting activities send fast signals along big nerve fibers that close the spinal gate before pain signals can reach the brain.

question: Why does severe pain after belly surgery put a patient at risk for lung problems like atelectasis?

options.A: Inflammation travels straight from the belly to the lungs
options.B: High blood pressure fills the lungs with fluid
options.C: Patients take shallow breaths and avoid coughing to protect their stitches
options.D: Pain meds paralyze the breathing muscles

explanation: When it hurts to move your tummy, you naturally take shallow breaths. This prevents deep breaths, causing tiny air sacs in the lungs to collapse.

question: A patient with uncontrolled pain has a high heart rate and high blood pressure. Which system is causing this?
explanation: Pain is stressful! It activates the sympathetic 'fight-or-flight' response, releasing hormones that speed up your heart and raise your blood pressure.

question: After giving a patient pain medication through an IV, when is the best time for a nurse to check if it worked?

options.C: At the end of the shift

explanation: IV medications enter the bloodstream immediately, so you should check back in 15 to 30 minutes to make sure the pain is going down safely.

question: What is a key way a nurse advocates for a patient with poorly controlled pain?

options.A: Checking vital signs and ignoring what the patient says
options.B: Telling the patient to endure the pain so they don't get used to drugs
options.C: Waiting until the patient begs for stronger medicine
options.D: Working with the doctor to update an ineffective pain plan

explanation: As a nurse, you are the patient's voice. If their current medication isn't working, speak up and collaborate with the medical team to find a better solution!
